es: Redactar en tiempo limitado una respuesta completa con postura matizada, ejemplo, concesión, refutación breve y autocorrección documentada.

vocabulary.es: depender de, girar en torno a
influir en, inclinar la opinión de

teaching.en: In a timed answer, a rough outline saves minutes: stance, example, concession, rebuttal and closing, each with its own few sentences.
teaching.es: En una respuesta cronometrada, un esquema básico ahorra minutos: postura, ejemplo, concesión, refutación y cierre, cada uno con sus pocas frases.
teaching.explanationEs: Un minuto de esquema evita rehacer el texto a mitad de camino.
segments: In a timed answer, a rough outline saves minutes: stance, example,
concession, rebuttal and closing, each with its own few sentences.
teaching.audioText: In a timed answer, a rough outline saves minutes: stance, example, concession, rebuttal and closing, each with its own few sentences.

teaching.en: Good writers add nuance without losing their stance: I would argue that remote work helps, at least for tasks that hinge on concentration.
teaching.es: Quien escribe bien añade matices sin perder su postura: yo diría que el trabajo remoto ayuda, al menos en las tareas que dependen de la concentración.
teaching.explanationEs: I would argue y at least suavizan la afirmación sin debilitar la postura.
segments: Good writers add nuance without losing their stance: I would argue that
remote work helps, at least for tasks that hinge on concentration.
teaching.audioText: Good writers add nuance without losing their stance: I would argue that remote work helps, at least for tasks that hinge on concentration.

teaching.en: A short concession, such as Admittedly, open offices are friendly, earns trust, and the writer can then refute the opposing case on its merits instead of attacking the person who holds it.
teaching.es: Una concesión breve, como Es cierto que las oficinas abiertas son agradables, gana confianza, y después se puede refutar la postura contraria por sus méritos en lugar de atacar a quien la sostiene.
teaching.explanationEs: Admittedly reconoce un punto ajeno; la refutación llega con even so o however.
segments: A short concession, such as Admittedly, open offices are friendly, earns trust, and the writer can
then refute the opposing case on its merits instead of attacking the person who holds it.
teaching.audioText: A short concession, such as Admittedly, open offices are friendly, earns trust, and the writer can then refute the opposing case on its merits instead of attacking the person who holds it.

teaching.en: When a sentence overreaches, rephrase it in the open: It helps, or rather, it helps some people, and that is the point I wish to clarify.
teaching.es: Cuando una frase se pasa de la raya, reformúlala a la vista: Ayuda, o mejor dicho, ayuda a algunas personas, y ese es el punto que quiero aclarar.
teaching.explanationEs: Or rather corrige a la vista del lector y deja documentada tu autocorrección.
segments: When a sentence overreaches, rephrase it in the open: It helps, or rather,
it helps some people, and that is the point I wish to clarify.
teaching.audioText: When a sentence overreaches, rephrase it in the open: It helps, or rather, it helps some people, and that is the point I wish to clarify.

teaching.en: Every choice has a downside, and naming it honestly can sway a sceptical reader more than any amount of enthusiasm.
teaching.es: Toda decisión tiene un inconveniente, y nombrarlo con honestidad puede inclinar a un lector escéptico más que cualquier cantidad de entusiasmo.
teaching.explanationEs: Reconocer el lado negativo no debilita la postura: la hace más creíble.
segments: Every choice has a downside, and naming it honestly can
sway a sceptical reader more than any amount of enthusiasm.

teaching.en: In the last minute, a careful writer will revise the tense, the connectors and the tone, and mark each change so that the self-correction is on record.
teaching.es: En el último minuto, quien escribe con cuidado revisa el tiempo verbal, los conectores y el tono, y marca cada cambio para que la autocorrección quede documentada.
teaching.explanationEs: Reserva este minuto para la revisión final: es donde se ganan los puntos de precisión.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase presenta una postura firme, pero matizada?

choices.text: I would argue that a four-day week suits most office jobs, at least for a six-month trial.
Everybody who has studied the question knows that a four-day week is the only sensible choice.
It could perhaps be argued, by some, that a four-day week might suit certain jobs in some cases.

feedback.es: Defiende una idea clara y la acota con at least; la frase con everybody y only exagera, y la que acumula could perhaps, by some y might se cubre tanto que no defiende nada.

hint.es: Una postura matizada es firme en lo principal y deja un margen explícito.

prompt.es: Completa: «El éxito depende de cómo se reorganicen las horas.»

feedback.es: Hinge on es la colocación habitual para lo que depende de un factor decisivo: success hinges on.

hint.es: Verbo en tercera persona que va seguido de on y significa «depender».

origin.text: A shorter week is no magic answer. Its success ___ on how the hours are organised.

prompt.es: Ordena la autocorrección: «O mejor dicho, debería decir que ayuda a algunos trabajadores.»

answer.text: Or rather, I should say that it helps some workers

feedback.es: Or rather abre la autocorrección y la frase siguiente delimita lo que se dijo antes.

hint.es: Empieza por la fórmula que corrige lo anterior.

prompt.es: Localiza el paso que falta en este borrador de respuesta cronometrada.

choices.text: A visible self-correction that makes an earlier statement more exact.
A concrete example taken from the writer's own experience at work.
A closing sentence that sums up the writer's position in the matter.
A clear statement of the writer's own position on the question.

feedback.es: El borrador tiene postura, ejemplo, concesión y cierre; le falta el paso de autocorrección con or rather o what I mean is.

origin.text: I would argue that shops should close on Sundays. For example, in my town the shops that close on Sundays report happier staff, and their customers have simply changed their habits. Admittedly, some shoppers will be inconvenienced. On balance, a weekly day of rest is worth that cost.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué se corrige la hablante a mitad de la frase.

choices.text: She takes back the statement she has just made.
She moves on to a different topic entirely.
She narrows a statement that was too general.

feedback.es: What I mean is reformula lo anterior para acotarlo: pasa de «expensive» a «expensive for small shops».

origin.audio: The new scheme is expensive. What I mean is that it is expensive for small shops, because a large chain can pay the cost within a week, whereas a family business cannot.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada fórmula de la respuesta cronometrada con el paso que cumple.

pairs: I would argue that, at least for focused work,
Take my own office, where the Friday meeting was cut
Granted, the commute is tiring; even so,
Or rather, I should say some managers
On balance, the trial is worth the risk

feedback.es: Cada fórmula ocupa un lugar fijo en el esquema: postura, ejemplo, concesión, autocorrección y cierre.

prompt.es: Completa: «Las cifras rara vez convencen a un público escéptico; una historia, sí.»

feedback.es: Sway an audience es la colocación natural para inclinar la opinión de quien escucha.

origin.text: Statistics alone rarely ___ a sceptical audience; a concrete story about one real person often does.

prompt.es: Reformula con «or rather»: es injusta; en concreto, con el personal a tiempo parcial.

answer.text: The rule is unfair; or rather, it is unfair to part-time staff.
accepted: The rule is unfair; or rather, it is unfair to part-time staff.
The rule is unfair, or rather, unfair to part-time staff.
The rule is unfair; or rather, it is unfair to the part-time staff.

feedback.es: Or rather deja a la vista la autocorrección y sustituye lo dicho por algo más preciso.

origin.text: La norma es injusta; en concreto, lo es con el personal a tiempo parcial.

evidenceGroups: unfair to staff who work part-time

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere la hablante sobre su propia postura al terminar.

choices.text: She would let firms experiment rather than set one rule for all.
She believes that every firm, large or small, should adopt the scheme immediately.
She thinks that complaints from customers should decide the question in the end.

feedback.es: Concluye que no exigiría el plan a todas las empresas pero dejaría experimentar: defiende la prueba voluntaria, no la obligación.

origin.audio: I would argue that a four-day week is worth trying, at least in offices. A company I know of tried it for six months, and the number of people off sick fell by a third. Admittedly, some customers may be disappointed to find the doors closed on Fridays. Even so, that cost is small beside the gain in the mood of the staff. Or rather, it is small if the company explains the change in advance. I have noticed that plans of this kind work best when the staff help to design them. Overall, then, I would not insist on the scheme for every firm, but I would certainly let firms experiment.

prompt.es: Responde al caso con postura, ejemplo, concesión y autocorrección (240–300 palabras).

answer.text: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.
accepted: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.

In my opinion, closing the city centre to cars is worth a serious trial, especially on the streets where people already walk more than they drive. Consider my aunt's bakery: two years ago the customers used to complain about the noise, and the drivers would park in front of the door for an hour. After the street became pedestrian, the bakery sold more, and the pavement was full of families. It is true that a few elderly customers were unhappy at first, because they could not get close by car. Even though that problem is real, I think it is easy to solve with a free bus and a few parking spaces nearby. To put it more precisely, the real difficulty is not the missing road but the lack of preparation. Let me rephrase that: a car-free centre works only when everyone knows how to arrive. Admittedly, not every street can be closed, and a hospital cannot be cut off. Still, many centres could. All in all, the evidence I have seen points to a modest but clear benefit, and I would support a trial.

feedback.es: Una respuesta cronometrada completa tiene postura matizada, ejemplo, concesión con refutación, autocorrección visible y cierre.

origin.text: Caso nuevo con tiempo limitado: un ayuntamiento estudia cerrar al tráfico el centro de la ciudad. Da tu postura con matices, apóyala con un ejemplo, concede un punto, refútalo con brevedad, corrígete a la vista con «or rather…» y cierra con una conclusión. Tienes diez minutos.

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender la directora con su respuesta a la periodista?

choices.text: That the trial has been a great success for everybody.
That several employees are about to quit their jobs soon.
That the journalist has asked an unfair question.
That the trial has been acceptable, but not more.

feedback.es: Responder con lo que no ha pasado (nadie ha dimitido) sugiere un balance solo aceptable, y el cambio de tema confirma que no quiere elogiar.

origin.text: Three months into the four-day trial at a small design firm, a journalist asked the manager whether it had been a success. She paused, smiled and answered: Well, nobody has resigned yet, and the Friday complaints have more or less stopped. Then she asked whether anyone wanted more coffee.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Aunque me gusta la idea, dudo que funcione.»

answer.text: Much as I like the idea, I doubt that it will work
accepted: Much as I like the idea, I doubt that it will work
I doubt that it will work, much as I like the idea

feedback.es: Much as concede el gusto por la idea y la oración principal mantiene la duda, sin but.

prompt.es: Completa: «Uso el último minuto para revisar el tiempo, los conectores y el tono.»

feedback.es: El último minuto se reserva para revisar la precisión del texto y dejar constancia de cada cambio.

origin.text: I have one minute left. I will ___ the tense, the connectors and the tone, and mark every change I make.
